title: Bitumen vs Asphalt | What's the Difference & Why It Matters

TERMINOLOGY EXPLAINED
BITUMEN VS. ASPHALT: WHAT'S THE DIFFERENCE?

LAST REVIEWED SEPTEMBER 10, 2026 · PETROBIND EXPORT DESK

"Bitumen" and "asphalt" get used interchangeably in everyday conversation, but they aren't the same material. Buyers who confuse the two can end up requesting the wrong product from a supplier.

Request Bitumen Quote
View Bitumen Grades
BITUMEN IS THE BINDER, ASPHALT IS THE MIXTURE

Bitumen is the black, viscous petroleum by-product itself — the binder. Asphalt (or "asphalt concrete") is the finished paving material: an engineered mix of aggregate (stone, sand, gravel) held together by bitumen as the binding agent. When a road crew "lays asphalt," the bitumen inside it is doing the binding.

REGIONAL NAMING ADDS TO THE CONFUSION

In American English, "asphalt" is sometimes used to mean the binder itself (what the rest of the world calls bitumen), while in British and most Commonwealth English, "bitumen" refers specifically to the binder and "asphalt" refers to the paved mixture. PetroBind, sourcing and trading internationally, uses the international convention: bitumen is the binder buyers procure; asphalt is what a paving contractor produces with it.

WHY THE DISTINCTION MATTERS FOR A BUYER

A buyer requesting "asphalt" when they mean the binder risks a mismatched quote — an asphalt plant needs bitumen as a raw material input, not finished paving mix, which isn't something a bitumen trader supplies or ships internationally. Being precise about which product is needed (bitumen grade, not the paved end-product) keeps an RFQ accurate from the first message.
